questions.q: How does the summary say fear affects a shopper's thinking?
a: It can slow the rational parts of the brain
It sharpens logic and improves comparisons
It makes people ignore advertising entirely
It only affects children, not adults
questions.why: Lesson 1 explains that the amygdala's fear response is powerful enough to dampen rational thinking, which marketers exploit.

questions.q: What happened after a security company aired a frightening commercial?
a: Alarm sales rose even though crime was falling
Sales fell because viewers found it offensive
The company was forced to pull the advert
Viewers bought the product to protect strangers
questions.why: Lesson 1 says alarm system sales climbed 10 percent while the actual crime rate was going down, showing irrational fear-driven buying.

questions.q: What did research on young adults and their phones find?
a: The brain's love region lit up when the phone rang
Users felt nothing when separated from their phones
Phone use improved concentration over time
Only teenagers showed any phone attachment
questions.why: Lesson 2 reports that for 18 to 25 year olds, the brain area linked to being in love activated when their device rang.

questions.q: What did the rat study in the summary suggest about food cravings?
a: Food cravings lasted far longer than drug cravings
Food addiction was easier to break than cocaine use
Rats preferred cocaine to any kind of food
Cravings disappeared once the food was removed
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the cravings of food-addicted rats continued seven times longer than those of rats addicted to cocaine.

questions.q: Why does the summary warn about online product reviews?
a: As many as a quarter of them may be fake
They are written only by professional critics
They are removed after a product sells out
They always contradict the star ratings
questions.why: Lesson 3 says up to 25 percent of reviews are fake, part of the manufactured peer pressure companies use to drive purchases.
